title: Balance Is Something You Practice
bigQuestion: How does your body learn to stay steady on a board?

story.title: The Board That Stayed Still
story.kicker: On the classroom carpet, a skateboard waits. It will not roll. Everyone gets a turn.
paragraphs: Mr. Kim sets a skateboard on the reading rug. He gives it a push. The wheels barely turn. "The carpet holds it still," he says. "That makes it a good place to start."
Lena goes first. She wears her helmet. She puts her front foot on the board. Then her back foot. She wobbles. Mr. Kim says, "Bend your knees. Put your arms out." She does. The wobble gets smaller.
Next is Theo. He puts his other foot in front. "Is that wrong?" he asks. "No," says Mr. Kim. "Some people ride that way. Both ways are fine."
By the end of the week, everyone can stand still for a long time. Nobody got a new body. They just practiced, a few minutes every day.
story.think: What helped Lena's wobble get smaller?

lessons.title: Grass or Carpet First
lessons.mainIdea: Stand on the board on grass or carpet first, so it cannot roll away.
reading: On smooth ground, a board rolls with a tiny push. On grass or carpet, it stays put. The soft ground grabs the wheels. This grab is called *friction*.
So start on grass or carpet. Put on your helmet and pads first. Step on and just stand. You can learn how the board feels without rolling.
When standing feels easy, you are ready for more. Then a grown-up can help you roll slowly on smooth, flat ground.

words.d: the rubbing grab between two things that slows or stops motion

look.title: Push Test
look.text: Look at one board on a smooth floor. Give it a small push. It rolls far away. Now set the same board on the grass. Give it the same small push. It barely moves.
look.prompt: Where does the board stay still? Why is that a good place to start?

check.q: Why start on grass or carpet?
choices: You do not need a helmet there
check.why: Soft ground grabs the wheels, so the board stays still while you learn.

check.q: What is friction?
choices: The rubbing grab that slows motion
check.why: Friction is the rubbing grab between two things. It slows or stops motion.

check.q: What comes after standing feels easy?
choices: Rolling slowly on smooth ground with help
check.why: Next, a grown-up helps you roll slowly on smooth, flat ground.

lessons.title: Feet Over the Bolts
lessons.mainIdea: Put your front foot over the front bolts and your back foot over the back bolts.
reading: Look at the top of a board. Near each end you see four small *bolts*. They hold the trucks on. The *trucks* are the metal parts that hold the wheels.
Stand with your feet across the board, toes pointing to one side. First, put your front foot over the front bolts. Next, put your back foot over the back bolts.
Feet over the bolts sit right above the wheels. The board is steady there. Feet too close to the ends can tip it up.

words.d: the small metal screws on top of the board that hold the trucks on
the metal parts under the board that hold the wheels

look.title: Count the Bolts
look.cite: A standard skateboard: two trucks, each held on by four bolts
look.prompt: How many bolts sit under your front foot?

check.q: Where does your front foot go?
choices: On the very tip of the board
check.why: Your front foot goes over the front bolts, right above the front wheels.

check.q: What do the bolts hold on?
check.why: The bolts hold the trucks onto the board.

check.q: Which way do your feet point?
choices: Across the board, toes to one side
One foot on, one foot off
check.why: You stand with your feet across the board and your toes pointing to one side.

lessons.title: Knees Like a Spring
lessons.mainIdea: Bent knees work like a spring and help you stay steady.
reading: Stand up straight with stiff legs. Have a friend give a tiny nudge. You tip. Now bend your knees and try again. You stay up.
Bent knees work like a *spring*. A spring squishes and pops back. Your knees soak up wobbles the same way. Bending also brings your body lower, closer to the board.
On the board, bend your knees a little. Not a deep squat. Just soft, like you are ready to jump. Keep your back tall.

words.d: a coil that squishes and pops back

look.title: Stiff or Springy
look.text: Look at a child on the board on the carpet. His legs are straight and stiff. He wobbles side to side. Now he bends his knees a little. His body drops lower. The wobble gets smaller.
look.prompt: Stand on the floor. Bend your knees a little. Does it feel steadier?

check.q: How do bent knees help?
choices: They soak up wobbles like a spring
check.why: Bent knees squish and pop back like a spring, so they soak up wobbles.

check.q: How much should you bend your knees on the board?
choices: All the way to the ground
check.why: Bend a little, like you are ready to jump. Not a deep squat.

check.q: What happens with stiff, straight legs?
choices: A tiny nudge can tip you
check.why: Stiff legs cannot soak up a nudge, so you tip more easily.

lessons.title: Arms Out Wide
lessons.mainIdea: Holding your arms out helps you catch your balance.
reading: Watch someone walk on a curb. Their arms go out to the sides. Arms out make *balance* easier. Balance means staying steady without falling.
On the board, hold your arms out low and loose. If you tip toward your toes, your arms can lean back. If you tip toward your heels, they lean forward. They help pull you back to the middle.
Keep your arms soft, not stiff. Little moves are best. Big flapping can make the wobble bigger.

look.title: The Tightrope Walker
look.text: Look at a tightrope walker on a low line at a circus. She holds her arms out wide. She tips a little to one side. Her arms move a little the other way. She stays up.
look.prompt: Stand on one foot with your arms down. Now try with arms out. Which is easier?

check.q: What does balance mean?
check.why: Balance means staying steady without falling over.

check.q: How should you hold your arms on the board?
check.why: Arms out low and loose help you catch your balance with small moves.

check.q: Why are little arm moves better than big flapping?
choices: Big flapping can make the wobble bigger
Big flapping looks like a trick
check.why: Big flapping can make a wobble bigger. Little moves help you get back to the middle.

lessons.title: Eyes Where You Go
lessons.mainIdea: Look up and ahead to where you want to go, not down at your feet.
reading: Your eyes help you balance. Your body tends to follow where your head points. If you stare at your feet, you lean forward. Then you can tip.
So keep your chin up. *Look ahead* to where you want to go. Pick a spot, like a tree or a door. Keep your eyes on it.
It is fine to peek down to check your feet. Then bring your eyes back up. When you start to roll, looking ahead also helps you see what is coming.

words.d: to keep your eyes up on where you want to go

look.title: Find Your Spot
look.text: Look at a girl on the board on the grass. She stares down at her shoes. She leans and wobbles. Then she lifts her chin. She looks at the red door across the yard. She stands taller and steadier.
look.prompt: Stand on one foot and look down. Now look at a spot far away. Which is steadier?

check.q: Where should your eyes be on the board?
choices: Down at your shoes the whole time
check.why: Keep your chin up and look ahead to where you want to go.

check.q: What can happen if you stare at your feet?
choices: You lean forward and can tip
check.why: Your body follows your head. Staring down makes you lean forward.

check.q: Is it okay to peek down at your feet?
choices: Yes, then bring your eyes back up
check.why: A quick peek is fine. Then bring your eyes back up to your spot.

lessons.title: Regular and Goofy
lessons.mainIdea: Some riders put the left foot in front and some the right; both are normal.
reading: Skaters do not all stand the same way. Riding with the left foot in front is called *regular*. Riding with the right foot in front is called *goofy*.
Goofy is just a name. It does not mean silly. Lots of great skaters ride goofy. Lots ride regular. Neither one is better.
To find yours, stand on the board on carpet. Try one foot in front. Then try the other foot in front. Pick the way that feels steady. The foot in front is your front foot.

words.d: riding with the left foot in front
riding with the right foot in front

look.title: Two Riders on the Rug
look.text: Look at two friends on two boards. Ana stands with her left foot in front. She rides regular. Ben stands with his right foot in front. He rides goofy. Both bend their knees. Both hold their arms out. Both stand steady.
look.prompt: On carpet, try each foot in front. Which way feels steady for you?

check.q: What is regular?
choices: Riding with the right foot in front
Riding with the left foot in front
check.why: Regular means riding with the left foot in front.

check.q: Ben rides with his right foot in front. What is that called?
check.why: Riding with the right foot in front is called goofy. It is a normal way to ride.

check.q: How do you find your front foot?
choices: Try each foot in front and pick the steady way
check.why: Try both ways on carpet. The way that feels steady shows your front foot.

lessons.title: Practice Makes Steady
lessons.mainIdea: Balance gets better each time you practice.
reading: Nobody is born knowing how to skate. Your brain and body learn by doing. Each time you stand on the board, they learn a little more. This is called *practice*.
Short practice helps a lot. Stand on the board on carpet for a few minutes. Rest. Try again another day. Wobbles get smaller as you go.
Count how long you can stand still. Write it down each day. Watch the number grow. A wobble just means you are learning.

words.d: doing something again and again to get better at it

look.title: One Learner's Practice Log
look.unit: seconds standing still on the board
look.cite: Example practice log with made-up numbers to show growth
look.prompt: On which day did this learner stand the longest?

check.q: How does balance get better?
check.why: Your brain and body learn by doing, so practice makes balance better.

check.q: What kind of practice helps a lot?
choices: Short tries, with rest, on many days
One very long try and then never again
check.why: Short practice with rest, repeated on different days, helps a lot.

check.q: What does a wobble mean?
check.why: A wobble is part of learning. Wobbles get smaller with practice.

review.q: Where should you first stand on a board?
review.why: Grass or carpet keeps the board from rolling while you learn.

review.q: Where does your back foot go?
review.why: Your back foot goes over the back bolts, right above the back wheels.

review.q: What do bent knees act like?
review.why: Bent knees squish and pop back like a spring, soaking up wobbles.

review.q: Where should you look while you balance?
choices: Ahead, at a spot you pick
Down at your shoes the whole time
review.why: Looking ahead keeps your head up and your body steady.

review.q: Kai rides with his left foot in front. Mia rides with her right foot in front. Who is right?
review.why: Regular and goofy are both normal ways to ride.

review.q: Why hold your arms out low and loose?
review.why: Arms out help pull you back to the middle when you tip.
